one_liner: Binary translator that runs thousands of copies of a single-threaded Wasm program on an OpenCL GPU; per dollar it beats native x86 CPU VMs only on some compute-bound workloads.
what_it_does: VectorVisor takes an existing single-threaded WebAssembly module, translates it to OpenCL C and runs many independent instances (VMs) of it in lockstep on one GPU, with a CPU-like flat memory model and system calls forwarded through a hypercall buffer. Programs are served over a built-in HTTP endpoint: guests link the wasm-serverless-invoke crate, and a client posts batches of requests. It is a standalone Rust server binary, not a library. It also has a --wasmtime=true mode that runs the same module on the CPU through Wasmtime.
how_it_is_fast: Throughput comes from SIMT batching: thousands of identical Wasm instances run as GPU work-items, so a throughput-bound serverless workload (hashing, image filters) uses the GPU's thread count instead of 4 vCPUs. The translator adds memory interleaving (the --interleave 4/8 layouts) so that lockstep VMs make coalesced accesses, partitions functions into kernels, and supports profile-guided optimization through a separate vv-pgo-instrument tool plus wasm-opt -O3. The gain is economic (requests per second per dollar of a GPU instance), not lower latency.
when_to_use: Many independent, identical, compute-bound requests (password hashing such as scrypt, image blur or perceptual hash on raw BMP input) that already compile to single-threaded Wasm
You already rent NVIDIA GPU instances (T4, A10G, V100 and desktop RTX cards are listed as fully supported) and want to raise their utilisation without writing CUDA
Research or prototyping of GPU offload for serverless functions written in Rust, Go (via Asyncify) or AssemblyScript

Throughput per dollar matters more than per-request latency, and each instance fits the fixed per-VM budget readme.md describes (3-4 MiB heap, 128 KiB stack, 128-512 KiB hypercall buffer), with VM count bounded by GPU memory
when_not_to_use: Memory- or I/O-heavy workloads: in the paper's own data the GPU loses on throughput per dollar to a native x86 CPU VM on LZ4 (0.08-0.15x), Histogram (0.30-0.47x), Strings-Rust (0.27-0.37x), Blur-Jpeg (0.11-0.57x) and unmodified PHash (0.37-0.62x)
Latency-sensitive services: requests are batched across thousands of VMs, and readme.md says the approach is 'less efficient than manual translation'
Multi-threaded guests or VMs that must talk to each other: only single-threaded Wasm is supported and the maintainer says there is no inter-VM communication or synchronisation (issue #4)
AMD or Intel GPUs: the AMD Radeon Pro V520 'sometimes crash[es]', Intel GPUs fail beyond smoke tests, Windows is unevaluated
Production use: research artifact, last commit 2024-09-26, build breaks on Rust 1.76 (issue #5) and is pinned to 1.74.0

integration.form: standalone binary (Rust server built with cargo build --release); guest programs link the bundled wasm-serverless-invoke crate
integration.dependencies: OpenCL 1.2+ runtime, GPU driver and OpenCL headers; crates include wasmtime 1.0.0, wasmtime-wasi 1.0.0, ocl 0.19, tokio, warp; the benchmark pipeline also needs binaryen version_109 (wasm-opt), the author's wasm-snip fork and vv-pgo-instrument
integration.min_toolchain: rust-toolchain pins Rust 1.74.0 (1.76.0 fails to compile cap-primitives, issue #5); the evaluation AMIs used Rust 1.66, Ubuntu 18.04, CUDA 12 with NVIDIA driver 525
integration.platforms: Linux host with an OpenCL 1.2 GPU; full support on NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti, RTX 2080 Ti, RTX 3080 Ti, T4, A10G, V100; partial on AMD Radeon Pro V520 (needs --nvidia=false --patch=true) and Intel Iris Pro (macOS); Windows not evaluated (TDR must be disabled)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; guests must be single-threaded Wasm and VMs share no state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the same .wasm file runs, but it must use the wasm-serverless-invoke request interface, fit fixed heap, stack and hypercall-buffer sizes, and be driven by batched HTTP requests instead of a Wasmtime embedding API

gotchas: Headline harness finding: the abstract's 'up to 2.9x throughput-per-dollar compared with Intel x86-64 VMs' matches only Pbkdf2 against the Intel c5.xlarge native run (T4 2.93x, A10G 2.94x, derived from page data in benchmarks/2022-12-22-20:09:12). The same native Pbkdf2 binary on the AMD c5a.xlarge in the same dataset ran 1233.4 RPS versus 149.3 RPS on Intel (8.3x). Against that AMD VM the GPU gets 0.32x the throughput per dollar. The benchmark's lockfile pins sha2 0.9.3, whose x86 SHA-256 backend switches to SHA-extension intrinsics at run time when cpuid reports 'sha'. So the 8.3x gap is most likely SHA-NI present on the c5a's AMD CPU and absent on the c5's Intel CPU (inference). Excluding Pbkdf2, the best per-dollar result against the Intel VM is 2.14x (T4, PHash-Mod), and against the better of the two CPU VMs it is 1.79x (A10G, Scrypt).

The GPU-favourable rows are partly GPU-tailored variants. Blur-Bmp wins (1.02-1.60x per dollar against the best CPU) while Blur-Jpeg loses (0.11-0.57x). PHash-Mod wins (1.37-1.65x) while unmodified PHash loses (0.37-0.62x). Each GPU figure is the best of up to four configurations (interleave 4 or 8, with or without PGO); each CPU figure is the best of two VMs. Every configuration ran once (NUM_REPEAT=1, 600 s), so there is no variance data. The GPU invoker waited 1200 s for OpenCL compilation before it started measuring.

The CPU 'WASM' column comes from VectorVisor's embedded Wasmtime 1.0.0 with 4096 VMs on 4 vCPUs. It ran 2.6x to 26x slower than native (for example, Scrypt 5.3 against 33.9 RPS). Large ratios against that column therefore overstate the gain over a normal Wasm runtime; compare against the native x86 rows. The hand-written CUDA baselines were host-bound: g4dn.2xlarge, with twice the vCPUs, nearly doubled CUDA blur from 576 to 1119 RPS on the same T4. The 'matches CUDA' result therefore compares against an under-provisioned CUDA server.

In the current run_benchmarks_aws.py, the native-x86 imagehash result is written only inside 'if run_modified:'. A fresh rerun therefore produces no cpu_x86_bench_imagehash_0.txt, and make_figures.py would silently normalise PHash against Strings-Rust x86 instead. The published dataset does contain the file. Separately, running with --partition=false also requires --maxdup=0; otherwise the generated OpenCL fails with function 'redefinition' errors (issue #2).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings DTVM, wasman, KinoWASM, WasmKit and Cage are CPU Wasm engines that cut startup or per-call latency. Pick VectorVisor only when you have many identical compute-bound requests and an idle NVIDIA GPU to fill; for any single request, or for memory-bound code, a CPU runtime (or native code) is faster and cheaper.
verified_claims_summary: The paper's own data (benchmarks/2022-12-22-20:09:12, one 600 s run per configuration, AWS us-east-1b, rust 1.66 builds, prices $0.526 T4 g4dn.xlarge, $1.006 A10G g5.xlarge, $0.3785 V520 g4ad.xlarge, $0.154 c5a.xlarge, $0.17 c5.xlarge) shows VectorVisor beating the better native x86 4-vCPU VM on throughput per dollar on 4 of 10 benchmarks: Scrypt 1.55-1.79x, PHash-Mod 1.37-1.65x, Blur-Bmp 1.02-1.60x and Bill-PDF 1.31x on T4. It loses on the other 6, down to 0.08x on LZ4 (derived from page data). The abstract's 2.9x is Pbkdf2 against the Intel c5.xlarge only, a VM on which native Pbkdf2 ran 8.3x slower than on the AMD c5a.xlarge.
status_note: Stale research artifact (last commit 2024-09-26, Apache-2.0, 5 closed issues) that builds only with Rust 1.74 and needs about 24 hours of AWS time to reproduce. It is usable for experiments on NVIDIA GPUs, but its headline 2.9x rests on an Intel CPU baseline that lacks the SHA extensions the AMD baseline used, and against the AMD VM the GPU loses on that benchmark.
